name: Python
tagline: The language behind data, scripts and AI.
description: Statements, strings, conditions, loops, lists and functions — written and run in the browser.

lessons.title: Printing and variables
lessons.summary: Get a line onto the screen, then store it under a name.
objectives: Combine a name with a string

sections.body: `print()` writes a value to the console. It is the first function most Python programmers use, and it stays useful for the rest of your career.

sections.caption: The quotes mark a string. Without them, Python looks for a name called Hello.

sections.body: A variable is a name pointing at a value. Python has no `let` or `const`: you assign and the name exists.

sections.caption: + joins two strings. You cannot join a string and a number without converting first.

sections.title: Naming
sections.body: Lowercase words joined by underscores is the convention: `first_name`, `total_score`. Names cannot start with a digit.

drills.prompt: Which line prints text to the console?
drills.explain: `print()` is the Python way. `console.log` is JavaScript.
hints: It is a function call with brackets.

drills.prompt: Print the greeting exactly as written.
drills.explain: `print` takes any value and writes it to standard output, adding a newline.
hints: It is a built-in, so no import needed.

drills.prompt: What does this print?
drills.explain: `x` holds 3, and `x + 2` is 5. `print` shows the value, not the expression.

drills.prompt: Which built-in function writes a value to the console?
drills.explain: It is a built-in: available everywhere, no import.
hints: You used it in the last step.

exercise.brief: Create a variable called `name`, then print a greeting that includes it.
exercise.starter:
# 1. store a name in a variable called `name`
# 2. print a greeting that includes it
hints: Build the sentence with `+`, or with an f-string: `f"Hello, {name}"`.

checks.label: A variable called name holds text

quiz.explain: `type()` returns the class object, and printing it shows the class and its module-level name.

quiz.prompt: Which name is valid in Python?
quiz.explain: Names may contain letters, digits and underscores, but cannot start with a digit and cannot contain spaces or hyphens.

lessons.title: Strings and f-strings
lessons.summary: Build sentences from values without painful concatenation.

sections.body: An f-string is a string with an `f` in front. Anything inside braces is evaluated and dropped into the text.

sections.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
print(f"{name} is {age} years old.")
sections.caption: Braces hold expressions. The dot at the end is part of the text, not the expression.

sections.body: Strings have methods, called with a dot. `name.upper()` returns a new string; it does not change the original.

sections.title: Strings are immutable
sections.body: `name.upper()` returns a new string. Writing `name.upper()` on its own changes nothing — assign the result.

drills.prompt: Which line builds the sentence correctly?
drills.explain: Without the leading `f`, the braces are literal text. With it, Python evaluates what is inside them.
hints: The letter before the quote matters.

drills.prompt: Fill in the f-string so it prints `Ada is 36`.
drills.explain: Inside an f-string, `{age}` is replaced by the value. The rule: braces around the expression, no quotes inside.

drills.prompt: What is printed?
drills.explain: `lower()` gives `zuno`; `str(2)` gives `'2'`; `+` joins them. No space unless you add one.
hints: A number must be converted before joining.

drills.prompt: Which method removes spaces from both ends of a string?
drills.explain: `strip()` trims whitespace on both sides. `lstrip` and `rstrip` do one side each.

exercise.brief: Given `name` and `age`, build `sentence` with an f-string so it reads `Ada is 36 years old.` — full stop included.
exercise.starter:
name = "Ada"
age = 36

# use an f-string to build `sentence`
sentence = ""
print(sentence)
exercise.solution:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
sentence = f"{name} is {age} years old."
print(sentence)
hints: Put an `f` directly before the opening quote.
The full stop goes after the closing brace, inside the quotes.

checks.label: You used an f-string
checks.expression: chr(102) + '"' in __zuno_src or chr(102) + chr(39) in __zuno_src

quiz.explain: Multiplying a string repeats it. It is a quick way to draw separators.
`len` counts every character, spaces included: two plus three plus two.

lessons.title: Decisions with if and else
lessons.summary: Make the program choose a branch, and return early when it should.

sections.body: An `if` block runs when its condition is true. The colon opens the block and the indentation defines what is inside it.

sections.caption: Only one branch runs. Conditions are checked top to bottom, so order matters.

sections.body: Combine conditions with `and`, `or` and `not`. Comparison uses `==` for equality and `=` only for assignment.

sections.title: Truthiness
sections.body: Empty strings, empty lists, `0` and `None` are falsy. `if items:` is idiomatic for 'if the list is not empty'.

drills.prompt: Which comparison checks equality in Python?
drills.explain: A single `=` assigns. `==` compares values. `===` does not exist in Python.

drills.prompt: Print the grade letter for a passing score.
drills.explain: `if` opens the first branch, `else` catches everything left over. Both lines end with a colon.

drills.prompt: This block will not run as written. Which line is wrong?
drills.explain: `score = 82` inside an `if` assigns instead of comparing, and Python rejects assignment in a condition with a `SyntaxError`.

drills.prompt: What is printed?
drills.explain: 75 is below both thresholds, so only the `else` branch runs.
hints: Compare against each threshold in order.

exercise.brief: Write `grade(score)` returning `"A"` for 90 and above, `"B"` for 80 and above, `"C"` for 70 and above, and `"F"` below that.
exercise.starter:
def grade(score):
    # return a letter
    return ""

print(grade(95), grade(85), grade(72), grade(40))
hints: Each `return` exits the function, so no `else` is needed.

quiz.explain: An empty list is falsy. That is why `if items:` is the idiomatic emptiness check.
Python chains comparisons: it means `3 > 2 and 2 > 1`.

lessons.title: Loops and ranges
lessons.summary: Repeat work without copying and pasting.

sections.body: `for` walks a sequence. `range(n)` produces the numbers 0 up to but not including n.

sections.caption: The stop value is excluded. That is why range(3) gives three numbers.

sections.body: A loop usually carries a result forward in a variable declared before it.

sections.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 6):
    total = total + n
print(total)   # 15
sections.caption: range(1, 6) is 1,2,3,4,5. Both bounds count: start included, stop excluded.

sections.title: Endless loops
sections.body: A `while` loop that never becomes false hangs the tab. Always change the condition inside the body.

drills.prompt: What does this print?
drills.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 5):
    total += n
print(total)
drills.explain: range(1, 5) is 1+2+3+4 = 10. The stop value 5 is never included.
hints: List the numbers range gives you.

drills.prompt: Print 0, 1, 2.
drills.explain: `range(3)` gives 0, 1, 2. The argument is how many numbers, not the last number.
hints: The first blank is a built-in.
How many numbers do you want?

drills.prompt: Which built-in produces a sequence of numbers for a loop?
drills.explain: `range` is lazy: it does not build the list, it yields values as the loop asks.

drills.prompt: This loop never ends. Which line is the problem?
drills.explain: `count` never changes, so the condition stays true forever. The body needs `count += 1`.
hints: Nothing in the body moves the condition.

exercise.brief: Add up the even numbers from 1 to 20 and store the result in `total`.
exercise.starter:
total = 0

for n in range(1, 21):
    # add n only when it is even
    pass

print(total)
hints: `total += n` is shorthand for `total = total + n`.

quiz.prompt: How many times does `for i in range(4)` run the body?
quiz.explain: 0, 1, 2, 3: four passes. The stop value is excluded but the start counts.

lessons.title: Lists that hold real data
lessons.summary: Store many values, then measure and filter them.

sections.body: A list is an ordered collection written in square brackets. Indexes start at 0.

sections.caption: Negative indexes count from the end, which is handy for the last item.

sections.body: Lists grow with `append` and are usually walked with a loop.

sections.code:
scores = [72, 88]
scores.append(91)

for score in scores:
    print(score)

sections.title: Built-ins that do the work
sections.body: `sum(scores)` and `max(scores)` exist. Reach for them before writing a loop.

drills.prompt: What is printed?
drills.explain: `-1` is the last element. `-2` would be 88.
hints: It is the largest of the three.

drills.prompt: Add the new score to the end of the list.
drills.explain: `append` adds one item to the end and returns `None`. `extend` would add every item of another list.

drills.prompt: Which built-in returns the number of items in a list?
drills.explain: `len` works on strings, lists, dictionaries and anything with a length.

drills.prompt: What does `scores[3]` do on a three-item list?
drills.explain: Valid indexes are 0, 1 and 2. Index 3 is past the end, so Python raises `IndexError`.
hints: The error is an exception, not None.

exercise.brief: Given `scores`, store the average in `average` (a float) and print it.
hints: Dividing with `/` always gives a float in Python 3.

quiz.explain: Adding lists concatenates them. `+` on strings joins them; on numbers it sums.

quiz.prompt: Which slice gives the first two items?
quiz.explain: Slices include the start and exclude the end, so `[0:2]` is items 0 and 1.

lessons.title: Functions that return values
lessons.summary: Name a calculation once and reuse it everywhere.

sections.body: `def` names a function. The body is indented, and `return` sends a value back to the caller.

sections.caption: Without `return`, the function gives back None — a common source of confusion.

sections.body: Parameters can have defaults, which keeps call sites short.

sections.code:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

print(greet("Ada"))
print(greet("Ada", "Welcome"))

sections.title: Small functions compose
sections.body: A function that does one thing can be tested, reused and read quickly. Three small functions beat one clever one.

drills.prompt: This function always returns None. Which line is wrong?
drills.explain: The value is calculated and thrown away. `return n * 2` sends it back.
hints: The result never leaves the function.

drills.prompt: Order the definition of a function that greets by name.
drills.explain: Definition first, body second, call last. Python runs top to bottom, so the call must come after the definition.

drills.prompt: What does a function return if it has no `return` statement?
drills.explain: Python returns `None` implicitly. Printing that function shows `None`.
hints: It is the value of nothing.

drills.prompt: Send the value back to the caller.
drills.explain: `return` ends the function and hands the value to whoever called it.

exercise.brief: Write `describe(name, age)` so it returns the sentence `Ada is 36 years old.` using an f-string. Do not print inside the function.
exercise.starter:
def describe(name, age):
    # return a sentence
text = describe("Ada", 36)
print(text)
hints: Template literals do not exist here — use an f-string.
The full stop belongs to the string, after the closing brace.

checks.label: It works for any name and age

quiz.prompt: Why define `def add(a, b=1):` instead of `def add(a, b):`?
options: It allows more than two arguments
It makes b optional to return
quiz.explain: A default makes the argument optional at the call site: `add(2)` uses 1.

quiz.prompt: What does `print(greet("Ada"))` show if `greet` only contains `print("hi")`?
quiz.explain: The inner `print` writes `hi`, then the function returns `None`, which the outer `print` also shows.
